name: Babylonia
summary: A Mesopotamian kingdom centred on Babylon. It is known for Hammurabi’s law code and, under Nebuchadnezzar II, for the grand city whose walls and Ishtar Gate still impress visitors.

location.value: Southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), centred on the city of Babylon on the Euphrates.

terrain.value: Flat river plains between the Tigris and Euphrates, irrigated by canals.
terrain.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

climate.value: Hot and dry; farming depended on irrigation.
climate.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

resources.value: Grain, dates and wool; stone, metal and timber came by trade.
resources.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

disasters.value: River floods and salt build-up in irrigated soil.
disasters.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

population.value: No reliable estimate. Babylon may have been the largest city in the world at times.
population.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

urbanisation.value: Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II was a very large walled city.
urbanisation.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

disease.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

migration.value: Amorites founded the First Dynasty; Kassites ruled later; Chaldeans and Arameans settled.

economicBase.value: Irrigation farming, temple and palace estates and long-distance trade.
economicBase.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

tradeRoutes.value: River and caravan trade with Assyria, Elam, Syria and the Gulf.
tradeRoutes.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

moneyAndTax.value: Silver by weight (the shekel) and grain served as money; interest rates were regulated by law.
moneyAndTax.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

inequality.value: Hammurabi’s Code gave different penalties for nobles, commoners and slaves.

governmentType.value: Monarchy; the king ruled as the shepherd of his people on behalf of Marduk.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Babylonia (checked 6 Nov 2026); Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

keyRulers.value: Hammurabi (c. 1792–1750 BCE), Nebuchadnezzar I, Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE), Nabonidus.

succession.value: Hereditary dynasties, interrupted by foreign conquests (Hittites, Kassites, Assyria, Persia).
succession.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

institutions.value: The Code of Hammurabi (about 1754 BCE), one of the earliest written law codes.

stability.value: Sacked by the Hittites (c. 1595 BCE), conquered by Elam (1155 BCE) and Assyria; Babylon sacked by Sennacherib (689 BCE).

eliteConflict.value: Rival dynasties; Nabonidus was unpopular with the priests of Marduk.
eliteConflict.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

armyAndTech.value: Chariots, infantry, archers and siege warfare.
armyAndTech.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

majorWars.value: Hammurabi’s conquests; Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem (587 BCE) and fought Egypt.

territoryChange.value: The Neo-Babylonian Empire took over most of Assyria’s lands after 612 BCE.
territoryChange.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Assyria, Elam, the Hittites and Egypt. Ally: the Medes (against Assyria).

inventions.value: Advanced mathematics (base-60 numbers) and systematic astronomical records.
inventions.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

scienceEducation.value: Astronomical diaries were kept for centuries, and Babylonian maths was used to predict planets.
scienceEducation.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

openness.value: Absorbed Sumerian, Amorite, Kassite and Aramean culture.
openness.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

religion.value: Babylonian religion, with Marduk as the chief god of Babylon.

languageWriting.value: Akkadian in cuneiform; Sumerian for sacred texts; later Aramaic.

artsArchitecture.value: The Ishtar Gate and the great ziggurat Etemenanki. The Hanging Gardens are credited to Nebuchadnezzar II.

sharedIdentity.value: Babylon as the religious and cultural capital of Mesopotamia.
sharedIdentity.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

neighbours.value: Assyria, Elam, the Hittites, Egypt, Judah and the Medes.

ideasReligions.value: Its astronomy, law and literature (the Epic of Gilgamesh in its standard form) influenced the wider world.
ideasReligions.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

colonisation.value: Deported peoples, including the Babylonian captivity of the Judeans.

riseSignals.value: Hammurabi united southern Mesopotamia in the 18th century BCE.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Babylonia (checked 6 Nov 2026); Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

declineSignals.value: Unpopular rule of Nabonidus and the rise of Persia.
declineSignals.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

outcome.value: Conquered by Cyrus the Great of Persia in 539 BCE. Successor: the Achaemenid Empire.

sources.value: Cuneiform tablets, law codes, chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Babylonia”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Early dates differ by about 96 years between chronologies.

knownFor.label: Code of Hammurabi
knownFor.note: One of the earliest written law codes, carved on a basalt stele.

knownFor.label: Ishtar Gate
knownFor.note: A gate of blue glazed bricks with dragons and bulls, built under Nebuchadnezzar II.

knownFor.label: Base-60 maths & astronomy
knownFor.note: The reason we have 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.

knownFor.label: Hanging Gardens (legend)
knownFor.note: A Wonder of the World credited to Nebuchadnezzar II, though no trace has been found.
